title: Two-band infrared dip data cannot identify a common CPV color break when each epoch has a free slope
abstract: We audit 51 published dip depths of five complex periodic variable stars at 20 epochs. All 13 epochs with infrared data have exactly two bands. We prove that a common sharp break from 1.05 to 1.60 micrometers adds no independent information when every epoch has a free log-depth intercept and slope. Its effect is exactly absorbed by those terms. The result holds for arbitrary depths and positive definite error covariance. A numerical projection of a smooth break gives negligible information at 1.18 micrometers under nominal wavelengths and reported independent errors. This formalizes an ambiguity already noted in the source paper; it does not exclude a break or dust. A simultaneous three-band dip at 0.477, 0.913 and 2.09 micrometers would test curvature without a shared slope across epochs. For a fixed break at 1.18 micrometers and slope change 0.88, independent 3% relative depth errors give an expected separation of 6.00 standard deviations. Four bands with two on each side give local identification of both slopes and a free sharp break. These are conditional forecasts, not detections. We provide a proof, source-schedule audit, original code, aggregate results, synthetic checks and a separate-scratch reproduction recipe. Raw light curves, full bandpass responses and physical dust composition are not fitted.

citations.reason: Source Table 4, epoch structure and smooth break. Its text already allows slope changes as an alternative; we prove exact sharp-break nonidentification after epoch slopes are removed.
Dust column bounds from two bands depend on the opacity law; our audit concerns wavelength curvature across epochs.
Stellar surface color changes can alter optical dust fits; our forecast is for observed depth curvature, not unique dust composition.
Free dust column mixtures give a separate material inference degeneracy.
The source spectroscopy motivated population tests; our work audits the separate photometric color evidence.
